title: Support Vector Machines
oneLiner: Draw the widest possible street between two classes, allow a few cars on the pavement, and bend the street with kernels when a straight one won't do.

what.html:
A support vector machine (SVM) is a classifier that separates two classes with the boundary that stays as far as possible from the closest points of each class. Those closest points are the support vectors: they alone decide where the boundary goes.

Everyday versionTwo groups of people stand in a field and you must paint a road between them. Many roads would separate them, but the safest road is the widest one: it leaves the most room for someone new who stands slightly out of place. The people standing right at the kerbs are the support vectors; everyone further back could move without changing the road.

When the groups overlap, a soft margin lets a few people stand on the road for a price. When no straight road works at all, a kernel lets the SVM draw a curved one.

why.html:
• Robust boundaries. A wide margin generalises better to new points that are slightly different from the training data.
  • One best answer. Training is a convex problem, so it always reaches the same global solution: no unlucky starts.
  • Compact. Only the support vectors are needed at prediction time (a "sparse kernel machine").
  • Curved boundaries cheaply through the kernel trick; it works well even with small training sets and many features (text, images, sensors).

how.title: A line that says yes or no
how.html: A linear classifier computes w·x + b and outputs +1 if it is positive, −1 if negative. The boundary is the line w·x + b = 0. Many lines separate a clean dataset; the question is which one is best.

how.title: Pick the widest street
how.html: Push two parallel kerbs out from the line until they touch a point on each side. The distance between the kerbs is the margin. The SVM chooses the line with the largest margin; the points touching the kerbs are the support vectors. Remove any other point and nothing changes.

how.title: Turning 'widest' into maths
how.html: Scale the line so the kerbs are w·x + b = +1 and −1. Then the street is 2/‖w‖ wide. Making it wide means making ‖w‖ small, so the SVM minimises ½‖w‖² while requiring every point to be on its correct side of its kerb: y(w·x + b) ≥ 1.

how.title: Optimising with rules: Lagrange multipliers
how.html: "Minimise something, but obey constraints" is solved by giving each constraint a Lagrange multiplier (a price for breaking it). At the best point, the direction that improves the objective is exactly balanced by the constraint. Example from the slides: maximise xy with x + y = 6 → x = y = 3.

how.title: Only the kerb points get a price (KKT)
how.html: For inequality constraints the KKT conditions add one rule: a multiplier can be positive only if its constraint is exactly tight. So αi > 0 only for points on the kerbs (support vectors); every other point gets αi = 0.

how.title: The dual: everything through dot products
how.html: Rewriting the problem in terms of the α's (the dual) gives w = Σ αiyixi and a prediction rule sign(Σ αiyi(xi·x) + b). Both training and prediction need only dot products between points; that is the doorway to kernels.

how.title: A worked example by hand
how.html: Three support vectors: (0, 1) is negative, (−1, 3) and (1, 3) are positive. Solving three small equations gives α = (3.5, 0.75, 0.75), w = (0, 1), b = −2. The boundary is the horizontal line x₂ = 2, exactly halfway between the classes.

how.title: Noisy data: the soft margin
how.html: Real data overlap, and insisting on zero training errors overfits. Give each point a slack ξi: how far it has crossed its kerb. Points beyond their kerb cost nothing; points inside the street or on the wrong side pay a penalty that grows linearly, the hinge loss.

how.title: The C dial
how.html: The objective becomes ½‖w‖² + C·Σξi. Large C: mistakes are expensive, so the street narrows to classify every training point (risk of overfitting). Small C: a wide street that accepts some mistakes (smoother, may underfit). Choose C by cross-validation.

how.title: When no straight line works: lift the data
how.html: Map each point into a richer space, e.g. x → (x, x²). Data that were tangled in the original space can become separable by a flat boundary in the new space; back in the original space, that flat boundary is a curve.

how.title: The kernel trick
how.html: Because SVMs only need dot products, we never have to build the lifted features. A kernel K(x, z) returns the dot product in the lifted space directly, e.g. (x·z)² equals the dot product of all pairwise products of coordinates. Popular kernels: linear, polynomial (1 + x·z)p, Gaussian/RBF exp(−‖x − z‖²/2σ²), sigmoid.

how.title: Which functions are allowed?
how.html: A kernel must behave like a real dot product: symmetric and positive semi-definite (Mercer's condition). You can build new kernels from old ones: add them, multiply them, or scale them by a positive number.

how.title: A curved example from the slides
how.html: Blue points sit near the origin, red points at distance 2. A mapping Φ moves the red points far away (e.g. (2, 0) → (8, 10)) and leaves the blue ones. With support vectors (8, 10), (10, 8) and (1, 1), the SVM finds the line x₁ + x₂ ≈ 10 in the new space, a non-linear boundary in the old one.

how.title: SVM vs logistic regression
how.html: Both minimise "loss + ‖w‖²". Logistic regression uses log-loss: it keeps rewarding points for being further on the correct side and gives probabilities. The SVM uses hinge loss: once a point is beyond its kerb it no longer matters at all.

how.title: More than two classes
how.html: One-vs-all: train one SVM per class against all the rest; the most confident wins (scores 3.5, 6.2, 1.4, 5.5 → class 2). One-vs-one: train one SVM for every pair (6 for 4 classes) and let them vote (votes 1, 1, 4, 2, 4, 4 → class 4).

demo.html: A real SVM trained in your browser. Click to add points, then try: Separable data with a linear kernel (count the support vectors); Overlapping data while sliding C from 0.01 to 1000 (watch the margin shrink); and the Ring, which only a polynomial or Gaussian kernel can separate. With the Gaussian kernel, a large γ makes islands around single points: overfitting you can see.

example.html:
Movie genres. The slides' multi-class example: predict which genre (action, drama, indie, thriller) a viewer likes best by combining several two-class SVMs.

Text and images. SVMs with linear kernels were the standard for spam filtering and document categorisation (thousands of word features, few examples); RBF SVMs were widely used for handwritten digits.

Supplementary In telecom, an SVM can flag whether a cell's hourly KPIs (drop rate, RSRP, throughput) look normal or faulty, with C tuned so that the boundary isn't dragged around by a few noisy hours.

misunderstandings: All training points shape the SVM boundary.
Only the support vectors do; points beyond the margin have α = 0 and can be removed.
A larger C always gives a better model.
Large C reduces training errors but narrows the margin and can overfit; tune C on validation data.
The kernel trick computes the high-dimensional features.
It computes their dot product directly and never builds the features.
SVM outputs probabilities like logistic regression.
It outputs a signed score; probabilities need an extra calibration step (e.g. Platt scaling).
Feature scaling doesn't matter for SVMs.
It does: the margin and the RBF kernel depend on distances, so standardise features.
takeaways: An SVM picks the separating boundary with the maximum margin 2/‖w‖; the points on the margin are the support vectors.
Training minimises ½‖w‖² subject to y(w·x + b) ≥ 1: a convex quadratic program solved via Lagrange multipliers and KKT.
The dual needs only dot products; α > 0 only for support vectors, and w = Σ αᵢyᵢxᵢ.
Soft margins add slack ξ with penalty C (hinge loss); C trades margin width against training errors.
Kernels give non-linear boundaries without building features; multi-class uses one-vs-all or one-vs-one.
thirty: A support vector machine separates two classes with the widest possible margin. Scaling the boundary so the margins are w·x + b = ±1 makes the width 2/‖w‖, so training minimises ½‖w‖² subject to every point being on the right side of its margin. Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions show that only the points on the margin, the support vectors, have non-zero weights. For noisy data, slack variables and the parameter C allow some violations through the hinge loss. Since everything depends on dot products, kernels such as polynomial or Gaussian give curved boundaries cheaply. Several binary SVMs handle multiple classes.
